How NoCharge tests browser games

A plain-language map of the project’s automated checks and their limits. A passing suite covers only the assertions and routes it actually exercised.

By NoCharge·Reviewed by NoCharge·Published August 19, 2026·Updated November 24, 2026·2 min read

Open the ArcadeReview PrivacyKeyboard-only play notes

Bottom line: NoCharge V2 uses several automated layers: TypeScript checking, a production build and prerender, content-registry checks, static ad-placement checks, Experience-route checks, asset checks, and Playwright browser suites. The repository’s npm test script chains the configured checks.

What the suites exercise

The content checks inspect published route records, metadata, internal links, generated HTML, and the Quiet Setup feed. Asset checks compare the approved asset registry with source files. Browser suites visit selected routes and exercise configured content, engine-loading, ad-placement, asset, Experience-route, theme, viewport, and calendar scenarios.

Each assertion has a defined scope. A browser suite can verify the scenarios it runs; it cannot prove that every device, browser, screen reader, or user workflow has been manually tested. Likewise, a static ad check does not activate monetization or approve disclosure language.

Keep release gates separate

Automated test output records only the scenarios exercised. It does not activate redirects, change DNS, deploy the site, add a publisher ID, or enable ads; production release operations are handled separately.

After source changes, rerun the relevant suites against the new build. Historical passes are useful evidence for the version they tested, not a substitute for current Batch 3 validation.
